Okay [Thread]: Tanto a música como a dança podem ser formas de nos exprimirmos. Se eu tiver um “quadro” de sentimentos, impressões e intuições na minha cabeça,  quando me exprimo, é para o comunicar. É para para criar uma representação interpretável daquilo que sinto. https://t.co/3P6pHuxMaN

A forma de expressão mais comum entre humanos é capaz de ser a verbal/escrita. Consegue-se argumentar que ela evoluiu para auxiliar humanos a sobreviver no mundo. Por isso é muito boa a falar do exterior, a comunicar comportamentos, a expressar silogismos lógicos.

No entanto, é mesmo difícil comunicar sentimentos complexos que não tenham termos conhecidos (feliz, melancólico). Isto pode muito bem ser por não ter evoluído um vocabulário suficientemente bom para falar da nossa vida interna e se o tivéssemos, dava. Mas tb pode n ser só isso.

Uma linguagem tem certas regras e características que regem aquilo que ela consegue representar, e com quanto esforço/complexidade. Coisas como funções sintáticas, combinação de elementos mais pequenos, as “mecânicas” da linguagem if you will
@ttrincea Então colega?

A pergunta é sobre se estas duas “linguagens” são equivalentes naquilo que conseguem em teoria representar, se são especiais e objectos disjuntos, ou qq que seja a relação entre eles

Has anyone else found themselves almost involuntarily interpreting everything through an evolutionary lens? My own psychology, social behavior, instincts, biology...

I'm sort of worried

I like thinking evolutionarily, I find it's a powerful sense making tool and the impulse drives a lot of knowledge compression. 
But most of the insights anyone gets that "fit" an evolutionary paradigm are probably wrong.
They can be wrong but still in a general direction that is useful, but some might fit and be dead wrong, in a completely opposite direction.

The reason I find this worrying is that the fact that an idea fits evolutionary pressures makes it receive a boost in "confidence-level" inside my brain. 

The fact that wrong ideas also get this boost increases the variance of "truth" inside my knowledge base

This isn't necessarily bad, but it's kind of worrying because I don't know what sort of systemic consequences it can have. 

Humans didn't evolve with evolutionary thinking as a tool, so who knows what it can do to a belief system when integrated?

Safety measures might include developing some awareness of the fact that a belief comes from some evolutionary reasoning. This awareness might unconsciously factor in when estimating risk and confidence but who knows if it works

Another neat idea is related to what I said about humans not having evolved with the tool of "evolutionary reasoning".  

We're all cyborgs, in a way. At different levels, with different kinds of plug-ins.
I can explain.
An expression I'm into is "social technology". Democracy is a social technology. The convention of tipping your waiter is a social technology. A framework like communism, etc

I mention this because I want to frame some ideas as "Mental technology". Like evolutionary reasoning, or Calculus, or food recipes.

They're not knowledge that you just read and write. They're programs, little scripts you install and integrate into your daily life.
https://t.co/UCvRPjQtoU
In this way, even if mental tech is not made of metal powered by electricity, it's still a somewhat fixed logical procedure that augments your capabilities beyond what you were born with.

You learn them, but there's a difference between developing your own mental tools by learning from your environment, and just "installing" one made by somebody else.

See GTD as a task management framework, or @swardley maps
In this sense we're cyborgs. Each with our own thinking modules installed.

So I'm into thinking about AGI future, and care about long-term risk from AI. As a result, I've slowly been loading the "AI Risk" memeplex onto my brain, and it's getting to a point where at least a skeleton is fully built.

I see a few problems with this.

If the structure of the ai risk debates gets mirrored into my brain, this can mean that

a) I get an expansive model I can play with and draw from while maintaining an outside perspective
b) The structure overwhelms my own ideas and I get "stuck" into existing modes of thinking

I also question the worth of seeking an overarching structural view of the problem and hypotheses that exist.

I'd probably be better off on the short/mid term if I focused on a local problem and worked on it while absorbing info from neighboring problems.

I've spent a few hundreds of hours reading and taking notes on AI risk. 

I find it fun, but I don't think I'd be doing it as much if it weren't interweaved with my school and (potential) career.

So I worry that an unusually large part of my identity will become tied to AI risk
What's more, much of this memeplex has strong taste from other communities (to which I regulate my exposure) and I'm not sure how much of those ends up seeping inadvertently into my brain.
It also stings that I'm devoting such a large chunk of myself to this and I still haven't contributed anything of substance, but I'll worry about that a bit later.

A positive aspect of all this "loading the AI risk model" is that I'm becoming more resistant to privileging expert opinion on what I should be researching, and a bit more confident in the quality of my own questions.
Although I expect that the more I work, especially with an intent to share and publish, the more I'll realize how little I know, and perhaps I should start that process now rather than later.

Trees "explore" possibility space and make you aware of the path of least resistance.

It's certainly less stressful, and seems more adapted to the "thinking in stories" most humans use to convey and preserve information

A THREADHELPER 🧵FROM @nosilverv & @ExGenesis 

TH right now is a humble intervention on the Twitter experience.
At a human level, it saves you search time and surprises you with relevant tweets
At a system level, it redirects the flow of attention to IRRIGATE THE PAST.

🧵1/17

The immediate benefit is that it works as a SERENDIPITY ENGINE that also saves you a bunch of time every time in search. Searching bookmarks is insane, they tend to be your highest quality subset of tweets. 

Showing random tweets when idle helps you find forgotten gems.

🧵2/17

In general, seeing your old tweets pop up feels like collaborating with past versions of yourself.

https://t.co/I6VphvBuIY

🧵3/17

Twitter's focus on the present makes it so that attention flow is biased towards the now. The ground is tilted. 

https://t.co/dEiY4CD7Il

🧵4/17

Your body of work should be a living system but water is drying up nearly as soon as it's posted.

https://t.co/SJuOptQAlC

🧵5/17

ThreadHelper works as a pump that redirects the flow of attention from the present to irrigate the past. You'll take better care of your garden, and others will pass by it more often. 

🧵6/17 https://t.co/BaFZ6MmIjH

The duration of your content's life is extended, it becomes viable to spend more effort on posts because we no longer expect them to be ephemeral as we get frictionless access to past insights.

https://t.co/gPi3PB5qi9

🧵7/17

As you do this, so will others. From a fertile ecosystem, desire paths emerge around the threads most traveled. Around those paths, "mindcities", scenes, new forks pop up.

https://t.co/oPWqMzAhgz

🧵8/17 https://t.co/hEUgODcBgp

Our plan is to become a "needle-shaped vessel",  a THREAD-SPACE-SHIP. Perceive and navigate this massive tapestry while interweaving your own threads into the mesh. 

🧵9/17

You'll be able to open full threads on the sidebar, with a tab interface that lets you shift click a tweet or QT to fork and see its thread. Also, you'll get a bird's eye view of threads you have open and how they intersect on a graph.

(mockup)

https://t.co/4UPAp2xtyN

🧵10/17 https://t.co/gP5X3hkENX

Less of a neat workspace, more a chaos-powered dashboard. Harness Twitter's dopamine mill and channel it into a massively collaborative ecosystem. Illegible wilderness becomes navigable-but-in-flux paths and structures.

https://t.co/IhV6JUr8kN

🧵11/17

Like Roam, but multiplayer-first.

https://t.co/KnL2DOtln0

🧵12/17

A bit farther into the future, we expect to be able to pull and search content from anywhere, basically a second-brain, allowing you to "search yourself".

https://t.co/xb18Ey1ZzR

🧵13/17

If you get tired BIG COMPANY TM, we intend on eventually adopting a user-centric peer-to-peer architecture a la Holochain

Your data goes from split btw different companies to associated with you and is merely read by services and other people. 

https://t.co/3oMWHVE0lE
🧵14/17

It matters to us that people remain sovereign and in control of their data. We'll help you store your data without compromising privacy.
By gathering data from different sources and letting people access and post it, a new context is born from the use that's made of TH. 

🧵15/17

We have a vision for a fairer, more human-centric web. This is just an example but recommendation algorithms are often exploitative. A market for modular, open-source recommendation algorithms that you can switch between at will incentivizes fair play in what  gets shown

🧵16/17

Eventually, ThreadHelper becomes a full-fledged vessel to surf and participate in the information web. The future is uncertain but having a trajectory feels right.

ThreadHelper open alpha starts today. Have fun!

You are what you eat. This is also true of where you point your attention.

Recommendation systems (RS) in social media are fundamentally misaligned with their users. 

The algorithm reads your mind and molds who you are. For profit.🧵 Here's how:
You might think the stuff you see online is pretty random, but it's actually picked by machine learning algorithms called recommender systems (RS). https://t.co/9CqpDj3uRZ

RS have their reasons to pick what they show you, and they aren't prioritizing user happiness. 

They benefit their operators by maximizing metrics: "user retention" or "ad-clicks". Whatever it takes to make those numbers go up. https://t.co/VgRNBAaDM5
An RS can use coercive, deceptive, and persuasive action to reach its goals. This is bad on its own, but the devil is in the second-order effects. https://t.co/sZMoBKLsIo
RS learn, so they pick up on the fact that users change based on what they see and nudge them to do whatever's most useful.
Little nudges over many interactions compound into significant change in beliefs, preferences, and behavior.
With 59% of world population online, it's easy to see the potential for catastrophe when centralized systems have a say in the construction of individual user identities. https://t.co/YqIgHUPVPj
We could ban RS, but then we'd be left with intractable oceans of information. We need RS to find stuff for us.
We could train RS to explicitly maximize aggregate human flourishing, but it turns out we can't really put that into maths yet. https://t.co/XrhvgZXp8A

What we can do is change system architecture
Recommender markets! Make them compete!
RS are controlled by a handful of corporations online, which gives them some freedom from the consequences of fuckery.
My hunch is that we'd get a better deal if you could easily swap which algorithm you're using. You're unhappy? Use another one. Want absolute control over what you see? Get NO recommendations!
Framed as a generic problem, we have networks of generic interacting agents, whose access to each other is mediated by an all-seeing learning algorithm. https://t.co/IYgx4EWUBs
We want to compare how populations fare under the absence of RS, a single unchallenged RS, and a scenario of competition.

Our model needs to implement a few concepts:
1. Welfare for agents;
2. Interaction between agents;
3. recommendation or mediation
4. Self-interest for mediators
5. Agent beliefs,
6. Agent preferences
7. Competition between mediators.

In my model, connected agents play prisoner's dilemmas(2) that yield payoffs(1). Agents can rewire their social connections - mediators as rewiring strategies(3) that can be replaced based on how well the agent is doing(7). Mediator self-interest lies in being used(4).
I still haven't settled on how to represent beliefs and preferences, but I'm hoping light will come from playing around with simulations.

(thesis time) Since we're done with our base model for agent interaction in a network, let's recap

https://t.co/BTiG8uCOWk

The Problem

The reward functions used to train current RS (ad-clicks, user retention) are misaligned with the best interests of users. (This problem generalizes beyond social networks to any mediated ecosystem.)
Because of [[Goodhart's Law]], it's hard to find functions that would be aligned long-term.
We need a meta reward function to keep picking the best ones.
A good one would be a market for RS, in a world where people can easily swap which one they're using to organize content from each platform.
A stylized way to model competition between RS with different reward functions would be cool. There are many possible such models.

The Model

 A few requirements: Users only have local information, interact with each other for reward, and can ask a mediator for recommendations. The mediator has global information, its own reward function, and makes recommendations to users.

Looking for base models I considered [[Sugarscape]], multi-armed bandits, but ended up settling on 2x2 games in networks. Specifically I'm using the model from [[Cooperation Prevails When Individuals Adjust Their Social Ties]] as a base.

https://t.co/jLRufcDw9W
Mixed-motive games like the [PD]([[prisoner’s dilemma]]) seem like a decent abstraction for an interaction between two parties.
Networks add a notion of topology that reflects how agents (humans and not humans) organize in the world.
Usually, models of RS have users and items which are recommended, but for simplicity we can interpret that a user seeing an item from another user is a proxy-interaction between them.
So users are recommended to other users, who can rewire one of their edges in the network to a new neighbor.

Our base model may be too simple: if self-interested RS lead to the same outcomes as perfectly aligned RS.

I expect that it'll be enough and that the self-interested mediator is gonna make the network unstable.
However, in such a case, instead of using strategy as the only parameter for a user, we can require that agents have preferences and/or beliefs

Finally bullish on dissertation bc deliverable products:

1. Model of Evolutionary Game Theory with mediation

2. A model of mediator competition (trivial)

3. Network evolution

4. Training an RL mediator of EGT

5. Analysis of network evolution under mediation

1. Model of Evolutionary Game Theory with mediation

Mediator as a complex rewiring strategy. Instead of a node rewiring to a random second order neighbor, it "asks for a node rec".

2. A model of mediator competition (trivial)

Basically EGT with rewiring strategies. Nodes have one from a few toy mediators (globally random, only rec C, only rec D) and change mediators if they're not doing very well.

3., 5. Network evolution

Just look at the parameters of networks under different mediators, pretty interesting on its own if not noisy.

4. Training an RL mediator of EGT

Arguably the hardest step. I'll be using a graph neural network (GNN) to process the environment and training mediators with reinforcement learning according to different reward functions.

Morning everyone, we'll be working in public today. Dissecting Threadhelper

writing up, summary:🧵

Lessons: fix scope early: easier than gradually expanding scope

Problems: local-first implies high memory usage; search could be better; important work is boring; crowding in the space of group cognition;  

Next moves: Sustainability and escaping Twitter https://t.co/60W26QAKnI

Lessons ☯️

the original thlpr thread tried to 1. give you a bit of our intuitions for how/why thlpr works and 2. show you how we can go from a small, high-leverage intervention to tackling our biggest problems.

https://t.co/0JZQE0wLWO

How it works: 
- Irrigating the past
- Taking advantage of Twitter as a substrate
- Harnessing the chaos to lubricate group cognition https://t.co/GoxyEqtZf2

Tackling big problems:
- Solving the probem of searching yourself by essentially building a data pod
- ...leading to decoupling data, apps, and recommendations systems to liberate the web https://t.co/PUO1OoBzuQ

The big-time has been moving slower than I expected. This is my first dive into production grade software engineering and unsurprisingly it's pretty hard. It's much easier to hack something to "just work" on your machine.

TH is made of a few components: 
- Sidebar
- Website scraper to inject the sidebar, detect actions like adding bookmarks, open tweets
- API scraper for getting tweets 
- Local storage in IndexedDB, keeping your scraped and archive tweets
- A search index

TH is local 

An early design choice was that TH would be local-first. 

Local has benefits: unquestionable privacy, search is blazingly fast, no money spent on servers; 

and drawbacks: all data is kept in your memory, and it's harder to manage databases

Scope 🗺️

I learned everything on the job. I went pure JS -> Node + Webpack for ES6 -> React in a webextension -> Pipes with Kefir.js ->  Functional style with Ramda  -> Typescript over that -> Tailwind for niftier styles -> Github actions integration for Devops
Scope is very important. It's MUCH easier to do something you've planned from the start rather than continuously expanding the scope of the project.

Performance 🔥

In most cases it'll be fine, but with really large databases TH can use a lot of memory. I have 22k loaded tweets and it uses 200MB of memory it's not dramatic  but there is some room for improvement..

One inconvenience is that uploading your archive leaves memory usage much higher and it only goes back when you restart TH/your browser. There's clearly garbage to be collected but it's really not obvious.

Again, memory goes way down if you just turn it off then on https://t.co/YZAYULJnII

Another inconvenience is that TH shouldn't be consuming memory when you're not using Twitter but it still does. 

This could be dealt with if we knew the meaning behind Chrome's "keepalive count" for browser tasks but to my knowledge there's no documentation on that https://t.co/9FFkGqLO1m

Search 🕸️

TH's current search is just our own configuration of elasticsearch and not good enough to just take whatever you're writing and show you actually relevant stuff.
You can get much better results by surrounding key expressions in [[]]. We're excited to roll this out, especially because of the interoperability with roam-likes it incentivizes.

Semantic search is another cool avenue we're working on. I expect it to make a huge difference in the quality of full-tweet search results. 

However, doing it client-side requires Web Assembly which is its own headache. Again, scope.

Twitter dependence 🐤🍳

Twitter API access is done through your personal authorization tokens, not the "apps" interface, so there's not a lot they can do to completely stop us from getting tweets, but they could still make it harder for us.

Some functions of the website scrape are built on hacks that could be broken by deep-enough changes to Twitter's interface. This reminds us that we're always somewhat at Twitter's mercy and who likes that?
However, we do spend a lot of time on twitter and there are so many small improvements or features that are only made possible by Twitter's design constraints.

Eg: showing QTs of an open tweet (implemented), searching based on the contents of an open tweet ((implemented), surfacing conversations with a particular open user, visualizing threads in space, keeping a vault of saved threads, harnessing the power of lists...
Sustainably supporting many data sources requires standardizing data formats and designing a canonical TH interface for displaying if we want e.g. people to contribute their own plugins.

@worldbrain is trying to do this with memex from a different angle, and they're farther along 

Starting on twitter, we focus on interesting UI experiments with constraints (tweets, users, not much else), offloading the bulk of the backend to Twitter, and migrating whenever

Friends 🤸‍♀️🤸‍♂️🤸

There are many worthy projects in the spaces we're interested in. Most of these aren't direct competitors, but we see them as at least partially addessing the same problems as us:
Searching yourself: @worldbrain, this project called dual https://t.co/T0rtFOKO1T and a bunch of other gpt projects
Group cognition: @RoamResearch @worldbrain, @NotionMagazine, @knovigator, @twemex (twitter only)
Decoupling data, apps, recommendation systems: @holochain, https://t.co/SDSaiSFPCp, @bluesky

Interestingness 🌋

I love playing around with systems, moving through levels of abstraction, designing high-leverage interventions, prototyping and refining them.

Plugin support isn't something I particularly want to work on. Neither is devops, or optimizing performance.

Actually, a lot of the work that would make TH robust and unquestionably dependable doesn't quiteexcite me so we should probably get some help in those fronts.
I've been on a clojure trip recently and I've built all of this in javascript 😿

Exits 💸

either TH makes money on its own, or we sell to Twitter, or we sell to Roam, or we stop working on it full-time and open source the code. 

If any of these happen, there will obviously be successor projects from me to address the liberation of the internet.

agents in a network play games with their neighbors
they can rearrange social ties for their benefit

SKILL: Structured Knowledge Infusion for Large Language Models

They're pre-training on knowledge graph triplets

https://t.co/UV1o0x5Y0z

1. models trained on knowledge triples perform competitively with models trained on natural sentences that contain the same knowledge

2. To prevent degradation, they mix the triplets with natural text from C4, 50:50

3. masking salient terms instead of random ones, improves performance on downstream tasks, so they mask either subject or object in triple

4. performance by model size suggests larger models benefit more from pretraining on larger knowledge graphs. largest model they test is 1B

5. there’s a big improvement in 1-hop questions, but notably smaller improvement on 2 and 3-hop questions. This suggests triples are not enough and some way to infuse more information about the graph structure is needed

ActInf book snips:

- action perception loop acts on goals, or info gathering

- strategies at diff time scales: evolution, culture, attention

- actinf is a normative theory: optimises a single value (free energy)

- it’s also a process theory for Bayesian brain

- learning and perception are the same at different time scales

- perception changes your beliefs to fit observations, action changes the world to fit your beliefs

- planning minimises expected free energy which decomposes into explore value and exploit value
- goals are prior predictions, planning infers an action sequence that fulfils this prediction
